item.title: Whatever Happened to English Summers? Scorched Britons Would Like to Know.
item.description:
As Britons swelter under yet another heat wave, forecasters are warning that a brutal summer is on course to become the hottest yet.

The Met Office, Britain’s weather agency, issued an amber warning — the second highest level — for Thursday in large parts of southeast England.

The extreme heat has remade summer for a country where many once escaped abroad to feel the blazing sun on their skins.

“An English summer is not the same anymore,” said Jacqui Browne, 67, as she sat on the brown grass of a London park.

On Thursday, temperatures in London are expected to reach 37 degrees Celsius (98.6 degrees Fahrenheit), according to a forecast by the Met Office.

There was a time when British summers were more temperate and marked by rain, but drought conditions have left large parts of the country parched.

The north, for example, is not as cool or green as usual, said Ms. Browne’s sister Janice Kennedy, 66, who was visiting from there.

“Even up north it’s quite warm,” Ms. Kennedy said. “Not like down here, but it’s quite warm up there, as well.”

Some, like Ms. Browne and Ms. Kennedy, still remember the summer of 1976, when repeated long spells of hot and dry weather made it the benchmark for hot summers. Now, that seems almost quaint.

The summer of 2022 stands out in memory for its intensity. It was then that Britain recorded a temperature above 40 degrees Celsius for the first time, according to the Met Office.

“Now it’s been overshadowed by the last three or four years,” Ms. Browne said.

By the end of this past July, Britain had already recorded 37 days of extreme heat, nearing a record set in 1995, when 39 days were recorded, according to figures from the weather agency.

Even if the last weeks of August are slightly cooler, the weather is still likely to break existing records, according to Met Office predictions.

“Another record-breaking summer now looks increasingly likely for the U.K., following the second-warmest June and second-warmest July on record, and yet another heat wave imminent,” Mike Kendon, the Met Office’s senior scientist, said in a statement this week.

“These statistics are a clear reminder — if one were needed — of the stark changes that we are seeing in the U.K.’s climate,” Mr. Kendon said.

Determining how a single heat event was influenced by climate change requires specific attribution studies. But scientists are certain that heat waves around the world are generally becoming more intense, more frequent and longer.

The heat has persuaded some to rethink how they spend their summers.

“I think you might find that is a real win for coastal towns,” Mike Jones, 55, said as he and friends cooled off in a London park. “I think there’ll be more staycations, too.”

His friend Caroline John noted a downside.

“When you go abroad, you have a cocktail and the sea,” she said. “Whereas, in London, you’re on the tube in the heat.”

The sweltering subway system is just one example of a region not built for heat, both agreed. Train lines have buckled in the heat, causing many delays over the summer.

“We’re not equipped, are we?” Ms. John, 50, said.

Britain’s weather agency warned that Thursday’s temperatures could affect heat-sensitive infrastructure in homes and businesses. And delays on the road and rail were expected, with potential health and welfare concerns for those stuck on the road.

The high temperatures could also lead to health complications for some, especially older people and those with vulnerabilities.

But for Anesta Logan, 61, who was in the park with Mr. Jones and Ms. John, the new British summer is an improvement over the cool ones she grew up with, to say nothing of the freezing winters.

“The hotter, the better,” she said. “People are always going to complain.”

item.title: What to Know About Today’s U.K. Special Election: Farage vs. Binface
item.description:
Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform U.K., Britain’s populist right-wing party, will face voters on Thursday in a special election that he initiated, hoping to return to Parliament weeks after resigning amid investigations into possible financial impropriety.

Mr. Farage, who is under investigation for failing to declare a 5 million pound gift (about $6.7 million) from a British crypto-billionaire in Thailand, has said he hopes that a new mandate from his constituents in Clacton, a coastal area in Essex, England, will show that his voters do not care about the issue.

He said that he has been the subject of “constant demonization” by the press and his critics. The investigations into his finances, he claims, are proof that the “establishment have now decided that they can’t beat us fairly, so they’ve chosen to use foul means.”

After he resigned to force the new special election, all of Britain’s major parties boycotted it, calling it a stunt. Mr. Farage’s most significant opponent is a novelty candidate named Count Binface, who campaigns wearing a trash can over his head.

Here’s what to know about Thursday’s vote.

As the leader of Reform U.K., Mr. Farage is the most prominent right-wing populist in Britain, focused on campaigning against immigration and in favor of lower taxes and fewer regulations, particularly on cryptocurrency.

A veteran politician who campaigned for more than two decades for Britain to leave the European Union, and who has led several parties, Mr. Farage is an ally of President Trump and has styled himself in a similar way. He has long warned of an “invasion” of migrants and railed against the establishment in Westminster.

For most of the last year, Reform led national opinion polls amid widespread concern about rising prices, taxes, migration and dissatisfaction with Keir Starmer, the former Labour prime minister.

In May, Mr. Farage led Reform to its biggest electoral success ever. The party won almost 1,500 seats on municipal councils. But overall, Reform won only about 26 percent of the vote, down from more than 30 percent the previous year.

And the party has lost several parliamentary by-elections that it had hoped to win in recent months, including in Gorton and Denton, which was won by the Green Party, and in Makerfield, where Labour’s Andy Burnham easily beat the Reform candidate.

The polls have shown a continued decline for Reform in recent weeks, as the accusations about improper disclosure of financial support have increased. Several recent polls have shown support for the party falling under 25 percent and Labour taking the lead.

Earlier this year, Britain’s parliamentary standards commissioner, Daniel Greenberg, confirmed that he was investigating whether Mr. Farage had broken parliamentary rules by not disclosing the £5 million gift from Christopher Harborne, the crypto billionaire.

Mr. Farage has said he did not need to disclose the gift, but has offered a variety of conflicting explanations for why Mr. Harborne gave him the money in the weeks before he won his seat in Parliament in 2024.

He initially said it was for his personal security amid threats. In his resignation speech, he said that he gets “daily online calls for me to be murdered” and has run up “very, very substantial bills to make sure that I was safe.”

But in an interview in May, Mr. Farage said the money was “a reward for campaigning for Brexit.”

Critics of Mr. Farage have pointed out that since he entered Parliament, he has championed the cryptocurrency industry and that Reform has pushed for light-touch regulation.

In his resignation speech, Mr. Farage referred to the standards investigation into the Harborne gift, but also said that “yet another standards investigation is underway.” That comment came days after The Sunday Times of London reported that one of his close aides, George Cottrell, had provided undisclosed benefits to Mr. Farage including security, social media employees and accommodation.

Mr. Farage did not intend to stay out of office for long.

In his remarks last month announcing his resignation, he said that “the people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions. This will be a people-versus-the-establishment by-election. It’s a chance to stick two fingers up to the entire establishment, to frankly tell them where to go.”

Reform officials were always very confident that Mr. Farage would recapture his seat in Parliament. The last time he ran in Clacton, during the 2024 general election, he won with 46.2 percent of the vote. The Conservative Party candidate came second with 27.9 percent.

But Mr. Farage and his advisers hoped to use the election to change the political narrative and give him a prominent victory over his major rival political parties. Instead, all of the main parties said they would not put forward candidates, preferring to wait for the results of the parliamentary investigation.

That makes it more likely that Mr. Farage will win a landslide, while making it harder for him to argue that he defeated “the establishment.”

Count Binface is a character played by Jon Harvey, 46, a writer and comedian who is part of Britain’s long tradition of novelty political candidates. He describes himself as an intergalactic space warrior from the planet Sigma IX. His campaign pledges include a promise to build “at least one affordable house” and to “cut your taxes and raise everyone else’s.”

Mr. Harvey — or, as he’s better known, Mr. Binface — has run in several recent elections. In the recent special election where Prime Minister Andy Burnham won with 24,927 votes, Mr. Binface received just 95. (Though that was more than twice the number of votes that Howling Laud Hope received as the candidate for the Official Monster Raving Loony Party.)

In a recent interview in The New York Times, Mr. Binface said, “If humans choose to vote for Nigel, that is democracy.” But with the major parties absent, “I seem to be his majesty’s opposition.”

He is not expected to win on Thursday.

Assuming that Mr. Farage wins, as expected, he will once again be a member of Parliament. But the investigations into his finances — and those of Reform U.K. — are unlikely to be resolved any time soon.

The parliamentary standards investigation could continue for weeks or months.

If the standards investigation concludes that Mr. Farage violated Parliament’s rules, he could be suspended, possibly prompting another special election. The Conservative Party has already said it would run a candidate in Clacton if that happens.

There is also a police investigation underway into the legality of two donations to Reform of £250,000 each from Mr. Cottrell’s mother, Fiona. In a statement last month, the Metropolitan Police said that two people had been questioned as part of the investigation, although no arrests have been made. Reform did not respond to requests for comment. Mr. Cottrell and Ms. Cottrell could not be reached for comment.

item.title: Israel Evicted Settlers Besieging Palestinian Homes. Hours Later, They Were Back.
item.description:
The Israeli military evicted on Thursday about a dozen settlers who had besieged two Palestinian families in their West Bank homes, but several hours later settlers returned.

The Palestinian families had been trapped in their homes since Sunday by Israeli settlers, who had erected a tent nearby and, residents said, attacked them, including with rocks.

On Thursday morning, Israeli soldiers dismantled structures set up in the area by the settlers, confiscated some equipment, detained one settler and dispersed the rest, according to a military statement.

The operation came after heightened media attention, including the disclosure that one of the homes’ owners, Louai Abu Ridi, 46, is an American citizen. Mike Huckabee, the U.S. ambassador to Israel, condemned the settlers and said the United States had urged Israel to intervene.

“The actions of those doing this to this family’s home is criminal,” wrote Mr. Huckabee, a longtime supporter of the settler movement. He said, “Actions by those who carried out this horrific act of terror meant to intimidate and harass this family are disgusting.”

But just hours after the eviction operation ended in the village of Qusra, located in the northern West Bank, at least nine settlers returned to the site where they were previously encamped outside one of the homes, according to interviews with two residents and video footage reviewed by The New York Times.

“We are still under siege,” said Yousef Hassan, 30, who remains locked inside with his brother and his son. “If the army is here to take out the settlers, why are they not just doing it?” he asked.

Mr. Hassan said his family was running low on food and water.

The Israeli military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The military on Thursday also evicted settlers who had taken over another Palestinian house in nearby Jalud, according to its residents. Here, too, the settlers returned shortly after.

The military’s failure to keep settlers away from Qusra village after waiting several days before evicting them underscored the challenge it faces in contending with settler violence. It also highlights the deepening chaos across the West Bank, where hundreds of Israeli settlers have terrorized Palestinian communities with near-impunity all year.

Extremist settlers have carried out at least 1,380 attacks across 250 communities in 2026, according to U.N. data from late July. Those settlers have faced a near-total lack of consequences for their violence.

Former senior Israeli officials who previously oversaw the West Bank now warn that the military is losing its grip on the territory and allowing settlers to run wild.

“The Israeli military lost control in the West Bank,” said Guy Hazut, a reserve brigadier general who once oversaw parts of the territory as a commander.

The settlers seek to drive Palestinians from their land and have displaced several entire communities over the past three years.

The families in Qusra have refused to leave their homes even in the face of persistent attacks.

“We are very afraid,” said Aisha Hassan, 35, who said she was still besieged in her home with her elderly mother on Thursday. “But we won’t leave. Even if it’ll get us killed.”

Adam Rasgon and Gabby Sobelman contributed reporting.

item.title: Electric Thrills
item.description:
It’s Friday, and as promised I have something fun for you: My colleague Chico Harlan, our global climate correspondent, is taking you on a high-adrenaline motorcycle ride through Lahore. And not just on any motorcycle. The bike he rode was electric — as are an increasing number of motorcycles on the streets of Pakistan.

Thrills aside, Chico’s reporting shows something intriguing: The war in Iran has sped up the clean energy transition. In the countries most vulnerable to higher gasoline prices, like Pakistan, the most common vehicles tend to have two wheels, not four. In those countries, the electric motorcycle era has arrived. Hang on tight!

By Chico Harlan

I went to Pakistan last month to learn about the country’s electric motorcycle boom.

Electric motorcycles scarcely existed in Pakistan three years ago, but now sales are surging. The switch signals how quickly, and perhaps permanently, people in developing countries are pivoting away from fossil fuels as the war in Iran keeps oil prices high.

I visited showrooms and an assembly plant and interviewed company founders and would-be buyers. As the trip neared its end, I figured I’d learned just about everything I needed to know.

Except what it feels like to actually ride one.

“Do you want take it out for a drive?” Abdul Rafay, the owner of a new Vlektra electric motorcycle, asked me after we finished an interview.

I looked out at the city of 14 million, as motorbikes pinballed around rickshaws and four-wheelers, and muttered something about journalists not making themselves a part of the story.

But OK, I’d accept a ride. I borrowed a helmet and climbed on the back of Rafay’s bike, just one among the hundreds of thousands of newish, gasoline-free vehicles humming along across Pakistan.

E-bikes and war

Electric motorcycles, it turns out, are a good indicator of the changes driven by the war in Iran. That’s because in poorer countries, where people are most vulnerable to energy-price shocks, two-wheelers are far more common than cars.

Electric vehicles typically cost more to buy than gasoline-powered versions. But rising gasoline prices have given electrics a big advantage: It’s much cheaper to charge a battery than to fill up a fuel tank.

In Vietnam, where the streets teem with motorcycles, the biggest domestic producer, VinFast, has reported soaring sales. In Kenya, about 25 to 35 percent of new motorcycle sales are electric, said Gagan Gupta, the founder of Spiro, the largest electric vehicle company operating in Africa. He said the war’s energy shock had helped “multiply everything by two times.”

People in the industry increasingly talk up the idea that future generations will never operate gasoline-powered vehicles. “The demand is effectively open-ended,” said Josh Whale, the founder of Ampersand, an electric motorcycle company that operates in Kenya and Rwanda.

In Pakistan, motorbikes make up about 80 percent of vehicles on the road and are often the most valuable thing a person owns. The new proliferation of electric motorcycles comes from a mix of homegrown ingenuity and China’s manufacturing prowess.

Some Pakistani companies use chassis and tires manufactured domestically, and batteries and motors from China. But other companies depend on China almost entirely. They import ready-to-assemble bikes that need little more than a logo. Pakistan, aiming to clear up its polluted skies, imposes duties of only 1 percent on such imports.

Sales of electric two-wheelers rose 173 percent during the first half of the year in Pakistan, according to a market data firm, thanks to a government subsidy program and the increase in oil prices that came with the U.S. war with Iran.

“Trump is the biggest salesman — salesman of the year,” said Muhammad Salman, managing director of Yadea Pakistan, the national distributor of Yadea bikes, one of the major brands in China.

‘You got scared, didn’t you?’

On the bike, I hung on tight as Rafay, 24, merged into a roundabout. We were in a relatively upscale part of the city, with painted lane markers and smooth roads. But drivers in Pakistan, I think it can be said, have a strong stomach for adventure.

Rafay clearly wanted to show off his new bike’s power. So he seized on a small opening and accelerated past a rickshaw. He zipped toward two orange vehicles, two or three feet apart. As Rafay darted toward them, a gap opened just large enough to let us through.

The video I was taking with my iPhone doesn’t convey my visceral certainty that one of those orange vehicles was going to clip my knee.

I’d clenched my legs hard enough that Rafay could feel it.

“You got scared, didn’t you?” he asked, looking back.

“Yes,” I said, heart racing a bit, but happy.

Rafay, a gearhead, said he’d loved his previous motorcycle, a Honda CD 70, Pakistan’s most popular gas model. He’d driven it more than 60 kilometers each day to and from his job as a software engineer. But then gasoline costs soared and he started thinking about the math.

“If I can save a few rupees,” he said, “I’ll do it.”

After my ride with Rafay, I thanked him for driving so capably and handed back the helmet.

Then, before the next rains came, I returned to the gas-powered Toyota car I’d been using for the week. It was a vehicle that never made me clench my knees.

Read the full story.

Europe sweltered in the fifth intense heat wave since May, with some temperatures soaring above 40 degrees Celsius. Some people in England are wondering what happened to their cool summers.

Vladimir Putin angered Japan with his first visit to islands the Soviet Union seized at the end of World War II.

Russian strikes on Ukrainian grain ships are once again threatening global food supplies.

An Australian jury found a former Catholic bishop guilty of sexually abusing two young Indigenous men in 2008.

The Israeli military evicted about a dozen settlers who had besieged two Palestinian families in their West Bank homes. Hours later, some of the settlers returned.

Social media tributes to Zhu Rongji, the former Chinese premier, yearned for a more hopeful era when the country was opening to the world.

My colleague Apoorva Mandavilli visited a factory in Brazil where scientists are producing mosquitoes that fight tropical diseases like dengue. Watch the video.

The most clicked link in your newsletter yesterday was about gadgets that keep you cool.

Although curling is decidedly a winter sport, a synthetic rink was set up in Rome in June. The surface is high-density plastic instead of ice. The stones weigh about a tenth of the regulation weight, and players use brooms to retrieve the stones rather than control their path. The goal? Get Romans to come out and play, despite the blistering heat.

Thousands of software developers across Africa have turned to Chinese A.I. models in the past year. My colleagues interviewed some of them to find out why.

Many developers said they wanted something that worked well on limited resources. They preferred Chinese systems, which anyone can download and modify without payment or approval. “Why use an expensive Ferrari to do the school run when a Toyota hatchback can do the same?” one Nairobi entrepreneur said. Read more about China’s A.I. surge in Africa.

In Bali, fireflies are revered as sacred messengers, a connection between living communities and their ancestors. But they’re disappearing across the Indonesian island because of climate change and environmental threats.

I Wayan Wardika has embarked on a quest to restore what he calls “the magic of fireflies.” He has started Indonesia’s first firefly conservation facility, where he breeds and raises them in terrariums named “honeymoon suites.” Read more and see the lab.

This version of the classic Southern lane cake takes all of fruitcake’s best elements — bourbon-soaked dried fruit, toasty pecans and shredded coconut — and weaves them into a rich, custardy filling set between three layers of tender vanilla cake. It’s a dessert and a nightcap, rolled into one.

Which island is this?

Naoshima, Japan

Sicily, Italy

Spitsbergen, Norway

Don Det, Laos

One of the things I love most about summer is that life slows down a little and I get to carve out time to read the books and listen to the podcasts that have piled up, literally and figuratively.

I’ll share some of my highlights in case you still have a bit of vacation time left.

My favorite nonfiction book this summer was “Peak Human” by Johan Norberg, a Swedish historian who tells the story of seven golden ages of humanity — including ancient Athens, the Abbasid Caliphate, the Song dynasty and the modern West. He explores what allowed humans to flourish in each of those periods and what we can learn from them today. (Spoiler alert: All of them were open to ideas and trade.)

My favorite novel was “The Safekeep” by Yael van der Wouden. I had to get used to the writing, which is sparse and self-conscious, and initially a little annoying, partly to channel the main character — a complicated, intensely controlling and, yes, annoying, woman. But two plot twists later, the book is kind of a masterpiece. The backdrop is post-Holocaust Europe. I won’t say more.

My favorite podcast was “The Gaza Chef,” a five-part documentary by Yassin Musharbash, an investigative journalist at the German weekly Die Zeit. It’s a compelling and balanced investigation into the death of Mahmud Almadhoun, who ran a soup kitchen in the northern Gaza Strip and was killed by an Israeli drone two years ago. I couldn’t say it better than the tagline of the podcast: “The question of why he had to die leads deep into the worrisome future of warfare.”

Musharbash once worked as a fixer for John le Carré and has written a series of novels himself. He knows how to tell a good story!

And finally, my favorite feel-good holiday song this year: “Love Chain” by Candi Staton, a summer classic. Enjoy!

Have a great weekend! — Katrin

Chico Harlan was our guest writer today.

We welcome your feedback. Send us your suggestions at theworld@nytimes.com.

item.title: Female Afghans Erased From Public Life in Five Years of Taliban Rule
item.description:
The Taliban regained control of Afghanistan five years ago this week, returning to power after two decades and restoring an Islamic government that had severely restricted women’s rights.

In those few years, women and girls have been systematically erased from most public life, experts say. And, some add, the limitations imposed on half the population could hobble Afghanistan far into the future.

The harsh restrictions on women and girls are a return to conditions that prevailed the previous time the Taliban controlled Afghanistan, in the late 1990s. More than 160 decrees have been issued targeting women and girls, barring them from secondary and higher education and restricting their employment, movement, dress, speech and decision-making.

“No other country in modern times has dismantled the rights of half its population through law, policy and practice to the same extent,” the United Nations agency on women said on Wednesday. “At the same time, overlapping humanitarian and economic crises and deepening poverty are also having a disproportionate impact on women and girls.”

The official restrictions have reinforced social pressures, and many women say their communities increasingly press them to conform, a new U.N. Women report found, based on recent surveys. “Half a decade of escalating restrictions has narrowed where Afghan women can go, what they can do and how they can live,” it said. “The results are alarming.”

The agency surveyed about 5,000 Afghans in rural and urban communities this past spring and last year, asking women and men about life under the Taliban. There were some similarities in the genders’ answers — but some very stark differences as well.

Many Afghans surveyed expressed disappointment with the course of their lives in recent years. Still, women reported levels of isolation and distress that suggest a growing mental health crisis, the U.N. report said.

More than half of men surveyed — about 55 percent — said their lives were worse than they had expected they would be before August 2021, compared with 65 percent of women who reported a similar sentiment. But their reasoning was starkly different.

Male respondents reported frustration with a lack of economic opportunities, while many women also blamed reduced access to education, for themselves or their children, and rules restricting women’s jobs and lives.

“By closing off education and many forms of employment, these restrictions compound the economic pressures already felt by most women,” the U.N. report said, noting the “profound personal toll” the situation has had on women in Afghanistan. Many women reported rising stress, worry and pressure, “consistent with wider evidence of deteriorating mental health,” it added.

The report highlights the isolation many Afghan women now experience as a result of the restrictions. A vast majority of the women surveyed — 90 percent — said they must have a male family member’s permission to leave the house. And more than half said they went out only once or twice a month. Among male survey respondents, more than 95 percent reported leaving their homes daily.

Women and girls’ adherence to the new Taliban rules is increasingly reinforced by people around them, like relatives and neighbors. The U.N. report noted that nearly 40 percent of women surveyed this year said they felt more pressure than before to tailor their behavior for fear that those they know will report them for inappropriate dress, speech or actions.

“The Taliban have extended state control deep into the private sphere by transforming patriarchal norms into legal obligations and conscripting families into the enforcement of their ideology,” Belquis Ahmadi, a human rights lawyer and expert on Afghanistan, formerly at the United States Institute of Peace, wrote in a recent report on Taliban rule.

Human rights experts say that the crisis for women in Afghanistan has reached a critical point.

Afghanistan is the only country in the world to formally prohibit access to education for girls and women beyond the primary level. The longer women and girls are excluded from schools, institutions and public life, the more entrenched the restrictive system becomes, the further behind they fall and the fewer models there are, making their ability to recover ever less likely, jeopardizing the country’s long-term prospects.

“As a new generation of girls grows without an education, their future becomes increasingly dark,” UNESCO wrote in a statement this week, calling for the full restoration of the right to education for Afghan girls and women.

Ms. Ahmadi wrote in her analysis, “Behind every Taliban decree is a human story: a university student packing away her books, a teacher dismissed from the profession she loves, a judge forced into hiding, a doctor prevented from treating patients, an entrepreneur closing her business, or a young girl asking her parents why she is no longer allowed to learn while her brother walks freely to school.”

She argues that the international community must speak up for the silenced.

“The greatest danger facing Afghanistan today is not only that 20 million women and girls are being systematically erased from public life,” Ms. Ahmadi wrote. “It is that the world is slowly learning to live with it.”

item.title: 8 Matisse Works, Looted from Library in Brazil, Are Recovered
item.description:
The police in Brazil recovered eight stolen works by Henri Matisse on Thursday, officials said, months after armed men made off with them from a library in São Paulo.

The police tracked the pieces, which belong to the French master’s 1947 series called “Jazz,” to an apartment in the suburb of São Bernardo do Campo, the São Paulo city government and the police said.

One person was arrested at the apartment on suspicion of receiving stolen goods, according to the police.

The pieces were stolen in December from the Mário de Andrade Library, São Paulo’s largest, during public viewing hours. Along with the eight Matisses, the thieves also took five works by the Brazilian modernist painter Candido Portinari, the authorities said.

In the heist, the men overpowered a security guard and two bystanders, according to an emailed statement from Rodrigo Bezerra, a police spokesman. Soon after, they were seen carrying the pieces around on the street in security camera footage released by the authorities. At one point in the video, a man places a stack of frames next to a pile of garbage on a sidewalk, then returns to pick it up.

The authorities in Brazil alerted Interpol after the heist because they were concerned that the pieces might be smuggled out of the country.

The police said that they had arrested one suspect in the robbery the day after it took place. It said that two other suspects in the library heist had been arrested in April in a separate art-theft case: a woman and a man described as the organizer of the crime.

Totó Parente, an official in the São Paulo government, said on Thursday that recovering the Matisse works was of “enormous importance” to the city. The police said that they had yet to locate the Portinari pieces.

Matisse’s works are coveted by galleries, museums and collectors around the world. And by art thieves.

His “Odalisque on the Terrace” was one of three paintings stolen from a private art museum in Italy in March. The thieves broke into the Magnani-Rocca Foundation and made off with the three artworks in just three minutes, the police said.

And “Odalisque in Red Pants,” taken from a museum in Venezuela, was recovered in 2012 by F.B.I. agents in Miami, who arrested two people and said they were trying to sell the painting.

It was not clear when “Odalisque in Red Pants” was stolen from the Contemporary Art Museum of Caracas because a fake version of it was placed after the theft.

The eight pieces recovered in Brazil on Thursday were “The Clown”; “The Circus”; “Monsieur Loyal”; “The Nightmare of the White Elephant”; “The Codomas”; “The Swimmer in the Aquarium”; “The Sword Swallower”; and “The Cowboy.”

item.title: Another Day of Extreme Heat Bakes Europe, but Relief Is on the Horizon
item.description:
Much of Europe was roasting on Friday in a dangerous, long-lasting heat wave — the fifth one on the continent this year — with the authorities in several countries warning of the serious risk of wildfires.

The scorching weather has strained infrastructure and severely disrupted everyday life and public services in several countries. More than 100 firefighters were deployed on Thursday to try and control a blaze that burned at least six properties in the West Midlands region of Britain, the local fire service said.

The heat, which has been linked to climate change, is driven by an area of high pressure that is colloquially known as a heat dome. This weather feature has been focused over the western part of the continent and is expected to shift east into Central Europe in the coming days, expanding into the Czech Republic, Germany and Poland.

Temperatures are forecast to slowly increase in Central Europe through the weekend and decrease to the west, as cooler Atlantic air and thunderstorms whip in from the west. It will still be hot in Spain and France, but the temperatures will not be quite as extreme as they have been.

High temperature warnings were in effect across Europe on Friday, with the most severe red-level warnings in portions of Italy and Switzerland.

Cooler weather was finally coming to some parts of Spain. AEMET, the country’s weather service, said that while the highest temperatures would broadly remain above 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit) across much of the country on Friday and through the weekend, afternoon highs around 25 degrees Celsius (77 degrees Fahrenheit) were expected on the north coast. Forecasters warned of a chance of thunderstorms on Friday, particularly in the eastern, mountainous part of the country.

Scorching heat has spread across Italy since last week and will continue on Friday and through the weekend, with much of the country likely to see temperatures between 35 and 39 degrees Celsius (95 and 102 Fahrenheit), according to the Italian Air Force Meteorological Service. Rains could cool some areas, at least temporarily, on Sunday.

Britain has been baking for days. The Met Office, the country’s weather service, said the country was on track to record its warmest summer on record for average temperature, breaking a record set just last year. Friday was forecast to be slightly cooler than recent days were, with the hottest temperatures reaching 34 degrees Celsius (93 Fahrenheit). A cold front was expected to pull fresh air into the country on Saturday, creating less humid conditions, forecasters said. There’s a possibility of some rain after the weekend and into next week.

Météo-France, France’s weather service, reported that the peak of the heat wave was Thursday, but much of the country was expected to see afternoon highs yet again between 35 and 40 degrees Celsius (95 and 104 Fahrenheit) on Friday. Temperatures are gradually predicted to fall, beginning along the English Channel and Atlantic Coast on Friday and spreading across the rest of the country through the weekend.

Germany’s weather service, the Deutscher Wetterdienst, predicted that the highest temperatures on Friday and Saturday could reach up to 38 degrees Celsius (100 Fahrenheit), particularly in the west and the southwest. Sunday was likely to be cooler, with rain in the forecast and the highest temperatures probably settling at 32 degrees Celsius (90 Fahrenheit).

Block out the windows in your home — especially those that get afternoon sun — with a blanket or a darker sheet during the day to keep the heat out. At night, keep windows open and run fans to circulate the air.

Spritz your skin with a mist of cool or room-temperature water or wipe your forehead with a cool cloth. Cold showers can also help you cool down.

If you need to be outdoors, put ice cubes in your water bottle and drink cool liquids. If you plan to exercise, douse your head in cold water. Swimming is also a great way to exercise and keep cool.

When exploring or sightseeing, seek out cooler attractions such as museums, cathedrals or even subterranean exhibitions. Some cities have created public spaces to cool down: Barcelona has climate shelters and Paris has drinking fountains, for example. London has a Cool Spaces map to find spots.

item.title: A Rapper’s ‘Diss Track’ Has Palestinians Asking, Who Gets to Speak for Us?
item.description:
The Palestinian rapper Shabjdeed usually makes gritty, defiant music about the struggles of living under Israeli occupation in the West Bank.

But in his latest song, “SLV," he’s turned his ire on a fellow Palestinian artist, a rising global pop star named Saint Levant. Born in Jerusalem, partly raised in Gaza, Saint Levant now lives in Los Angeles and is more likely to sing about his lovers than his homeland.

That appears to be Shabjdeed’s main gripe.

“Mixing Palestine with all kinds of bullshit and European pretentiousness, acting all chill,” Shabjdeed rapped to Saint Levant. “I’ll slap a watermelon right on your thigh — just so you know how much I love my country,” he added, a reference to the red, green and black fruit that shares the colors of the Palestinian flag.

The song, attacking Saint Levant’s persona and music as inauthentic, has drawn comparison with a similar, long-running feud between the rappers Kendrick Lamar and Drake. It has also struck a chord with many Palestinians, raising questions about their identity and representation, especially in the arts.

Palestinians have a long history of displacement, with no independent state or centralized political leadership. Who speaks for them — and how — has become a charged debate, and especially so since the Gaza war and rising Israeli settler violence in the West Bank.

Agents for Shabjdeed and Saint Levant, whose real names are Oday Abbas and Marwan Abdelhamid, did not respond to requests for comment. Both artists held competing concerts in Amman, Jordan, on Thursday night, with “SLV” included in Shabjdeed’s set.

Palestinian identity itself is complex. It has been shaped not only by a long history but also the forced expulsion and displacement of Palestinians by the creation of the state of Israel in 1948. The subsequent decades of Israeli occupation and further rounds of displacement have led to a fracturing of the Palestinian experience, with many forced to live far from their ancestral homes.

“Each of us carries a different piece of a puzzle that was shattered in 1948,” said Tamer Nafar, a rapper who is often considered the godfather of Palestinian hip-hop and co-founded the group DAM.

“The occupation dispersed us,” added Mr. Nafar, who lives in Lod, Israel. “It did not necessarily change our identity or our essence, but it certainly changed our perspective, our living conditions and the way each of us relates to Palestine.”

While the Ramallah-based Shabjdeed presents himself as the more authentically Palestinian voice, the pointed insults in “SLV” have led some to scrutinize his words and actions. Critics of the recent track accused him of not speaking out enough against the war in Gaza and noted that he continued to stage concerts during that time.

Saint Levant, 25, who often sings in Arabic as well as French and English, has made songs about Gaza and spoken out against the war during his concerts.

He has not responded to the dig from Shabjdeed, though another Palestinian rapper has.

Emsallam, a Jordanian-Palestinian musician whose real name is Msallam Hdaib, was the target of a Shabjdeed diss track in 2018. When Shabjdeed released “SLV,” Emsallam soon put out a lyrical response, urging him to rap about the war in Gaza, rather than going after other Palestinian artists.

“You don’t have any more honor — God, after this song I don’t want to hear your hisses,” Emsallam sang. “We haven’t heard your voice in three years amid all the massacres.”

Shabjdeed’s lyrics criticized Saint Levant’s focus on romance in his music, and his collaborations with Mia Khalifa, a former adult film star turned influencer and political activist, and the Lebanese pop star Haifa Wehbe.

Some Palestinians have pushed back on Shabjdeed’s criticisms, arguing in interviews and in discussions online that his lyrics feed into a long history of reducing the complexity and diversity of their lives to the political struggle.

“Palestinians are not a monolith, and we’re not all the same, and I don’t think anyone has a right to police who gets to be Palestinian,” said Tala Hammash, a fan of both artists, who runs a business in the United Arab Emirates importing pantry goods from the West Bank. “I think that’s one of the key pushbacks against the diss track against Saint Levant. So what if he talks about love and whatnot? Does that become less Palestinian?”

Ms. Hammash, who was born in Jordan and said she had not yet been able to visit her ancestral homes in Jenin and Jerusalem, added that art should grapple with every aspect of the Palestinian experience. After hearing the recent diss track, she posted a series of questions on Instagram.

“Is Shabjdeed a troll? Absolutely,” she wrote. “Are the criticisms of Marwan (SLV) valid? Yes.”

Those questions sparked discussion among her friends and followers online, and some said they felt Saint Levant performs for the tastes of Western audiences. Others said his success — from brand partnership deals to gracing the cover of fashion magazines — had come about in part because he is viewed as more Western than Arab, Ms. Hammash said.

Defenders of Saint Levant would characterize that as an unfair representation, arguing that he has put his Palestinian identity front and center. He regularly performs wearing the kaffiyeh, the black-and-white checkered scarf traditionally worn in parts of the Middle East, and waving the Palestinian flag. This summer, when he was named Prada’s new brand ambassador, he was pictured wearing a pendant depicting an outline of historical Palestine.

He has also said that his life’s goal “is to be the president of Palestine.” Saint Levant did not respond when asked, via his agent, about the criticism he had faced.

Mr. Nafar, one of the founders of Palestinian hip-hop, said that while he felt Saint Levant’s music was coming from a good place, his representation can feel simplistic, trendy and disconnected from the complex reality that Palestinians on the ground live every day.

Rather than shrink from the controversy, though, he encouraged Saint Levant to clap back and engage in a discourse that wrestles with questions of place, authenticity and who gets to tell which story, issues inherent to hip-hop, he said.

“As a rapper I say, ‘Yalla Saint,’” Mr. Nafar said, using the Arabic word for “let’s go.”

“Get your diss track back, and let the story go on,” he added.

Heedo Abu Laban contributed reporting.

item.title: After Notre-Dame Fire, France Restored the Cathedral — but Not These Windows
item.description:
Seven and a half years after a raging fire nearly destroyed the Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris, workers will soon begin installing the most contentious feature of its meticulous restoration: six towering stained-glass windows that depict the Christian feast of Pentecost.

Unlike the cathedral’s gargoyles, paintings and other treasures, which were refurbished, the windows are entirely new.

The work of a French artist, Claire Tabouret, they depict landscapes and traditional religious processions, but in a contemporary style. They will replace 19th-century stained-glass windows on the south side of the soaring nave, fueling a fierce debate over the ethics of introducing contemporary artwork to an 800-year-old masterpiece.

More than 300,000 people signed a petition demanding that the old windows be left in place, while preservationist groups filed multiple legal challenges against their replacement. They argued that it was a breach of France’s heritage laws, no small thing in a country that prizes its artistic and architectural patrimony.

“Demolishing the past, unraveling something that’s already designated as a historic monument, just to make way for something else — that’s pretty unprecedented,” said Julien Lacaze, the president of Sites & Monuments, a group that campaigns to protect France’s architectural heritage.

None of that resistance has been successful. The new windows are nearly complete and set to be installed by the end of 2026. Now, the officials overseeing Notre-Dame’s restoration are cautiously optimistic that, for all the earlier criticism, worshipers and visitors will ultimately welcome the latest addition to the cathedral, once they see it in place.

“It’s often like that,” said Philippe Jost, the president of the Public Establishment Rebuilding Notre-Dame de Paris. “Before, opinions are expressed, often in a passionate way, with the strength of conviction. Then, once things are there, people realize that in fact, they aren’t that bad.”

The windows are being made in a centuries-old glassmaking workshop in Reims, an ancient city 80 miles east of Paris. I visited it this summer with Mr. Jost, a tour that provided another twist in this tangled story. It turned out that the workshop, Atelier Simon-Marq, which was founded in 1640, is now tucked into the basement of a much younger church, the midcentury modern Église du Sacré-Coeur, or Church of the Sacred Heart.

The symbolism was hard to miss: A 1950s church, built of reinforced concrete and deconsecrated about 60 years after it opened, houses one of Europe’s oldest workshops. That atelier is in turn creating stained-glass windows for perhaps the world’s most famous gothic cathedral, the first stone of which was laid in 1163.

Inside the workshop, craftspeople hunched over light tables, painting and engraving pieces of cut glass that will be fired and assembled into the stained-glass windows.

The company was founded by Pierre Simon, a master glassmaker, and remained in his family’s ownership until nearly two decades ago. Over the centuries, it collaborated with artists like Marc Chagall and Joan Miró, and helped to restore the windows of Reims Cathedral after they were damaged in World War I.

After falling on hard times, the family sold the workshop in 2011. It was later sold again to two wealthy businessmen from Reims, Pierre-Emmanuel Taittinger, the former president of the Taittinger Champagne house, and Philippe Varin, a former chairman of the French automaker PSA Peugeot Citroën.

Mr. Taittinger, needing to move the workshop to larger quarters, hit upon the idea of putting it in a converted church. He said he thought this would provide a peaceful, almost monastic environment, consistent with restoring stained-glass windows.

Mr. Taittinger said he made his pitch to the newly installed archbishop of Reims, Éric de Moulins-Beaufort. “After one or two glasses of Champagne,” he recalled lightheartedly, “the bishop said, ‘Yes, I have one or two churches.’”

Later, Mr. Taittinger welcomed another archbishop, Laurent Ulrich of Paris, to the workshop. It was Archbishop Ulrich who first proposed replacing Notre-Dame’s 19th-century windows, which were designed by the French architect Eugène Viollet-le-Duc. The archbishop raised the idea with President Emmanuel Macron, who, eager to leave his mark on the restoration of Notre-Dame, embraced it.

After an international competition, the project was awarded to Ms. Tabouret, 44, a French artist who paints in a figurative style. She said she was intrigued, rather than put off, by the debate over installing new windows. “It’s not very usual that we do things like this in France,” she said. “That’s a very strong sign for the country, and for the church.”

Archbishop Ulrich, who suggested that Ms. Tabouret take Pentecost as her theme, defended the choice to go modern as entirely in keeping with the history of Notre-Dame. Since it was completed in 1345, he said, “the cathedral has been enriched, has undergone transformations and has welcomed them.”

Céline Bachelot, a manager at the Atelier Simon-Marq, said she was awed by the chance to create something that will become part of Notre-Dame. “It happens maybe once every two centuries,” she said.

Part of the optimism of the project’s backers stems from the positive reception for a recent exhibit of Ms. Tabouret’s full-scale sketches for the windows. Some 340,000 people visited the exhibit, at the Grand Palais museum in Paris, and the reviews in French newspapers were positive.

“My heart is beating a little bit,” said Ms. Tabouret of the year-end unveiling. “Obviously, some people won’t like them. You can’t please everybody when you have 15 million people a year visiting the cathedral.”

Ms. Tabouret, who recently returned to France after a decade living in Los Angeles, said she admired the passion that historical preservation aroused in the French. France, she said, was one of only a few countries where people could be overheard in a bar debating the merits of restoring old buildings.

But she dismissed the contention that her windows would erase the legacy of Viollet-le-Duc, whose windows were themselves part of a broader restoration of Notre-Dame. His windows will be restored and displayed: two at an architecture museum in Paris and four in a chateau north of Paris that he rebuilt.

And Viollet-le-Duc’s most visible contribution, the lead-covered wooden spire that rose above the cathedral’s transept, was rebuilt faithfully after it collapsed in 2019. French officials solicited cutting-edge proposals from prominent architects like Norman Foster before deciding to stick to the original design.

“If you go to the newly restored Notre-Dame, it’s an incredible homage to Viollet-le-Duc,” Ms. Tabouret said.

For now, though, she is more focused on finishing her own windows. In visits to the workshop every other week, she said she still tinkered with her designs. “I just changed some work on the faces,” she said in our interview.

“We’re working on the procession in the last window,” she said. “It’s the last image you see before you leave the cathedral.”

Reporting was contributed by Ségolène Le Stradic, Ana Castelain and Giulia Imbert.

item.title: As Europe Gets Hotter, Its Transportation Systems Struggle to Cope
item.description:
Tracks are buckling in Sweden. Highways are cracking in Germany. Commuters are sweltering in airless train carriages across the world’s fastest-warming continent.

This is the new reality in Europe, where much of the transportation infrastructure was not built to withstand the scorching summer heat that’s becoming routine.

“Europe’s transport systems were engineered for a climate that no longer exists,” Patrice Geoffron, who leads the energy and climate economics team at Université Paris Dauphine-PSL in France, wrote in an email.

Many of Europe’s tracks and roads desperately need upgrades to meet new extreme temperature thresholds, or delays and disruptions will become the norm, experts said. Rail services in Britain and France reduced services this week and warned of disruptions as Western Europe endured its fifth heat wave since May,

The changes needed to fully accommodate the effects of global warming would require vast amounts of money. And even if cash-strapped European governments had those funds, many countries are focused more on defense than on infrastructure, experts said. For now, they are mostly making smaller adjustments.

“The main challenge is actually not heat; the main challenge is funding itself,” said Prof. Felix Creutzig of the University of Sussex, who leads the working group on cities at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research near Berlin.

Disruptions from the heat are most obvious on Europe’s trains, which hundreds of millions of people use in cities and to cross the countryside. Many of these rail systems are generations old, said Ian Mulcahey, the global director of cities at Gensler, an international architecture and planning firm. (London’s metro, the world’s oldest, opened in 1863.)

Many of these systems still rely, to some degree, on dated infrastructure. Many European train carriages don’t have air-conditioning.

Some systems are incorporating new technologies as they expand and update. Mr. Mulcahey pointed to the air-conditioned Elizabeth Line in London, a major east-west artery that opened in 2022 and cost about 19 billion pounds ($25.5 billion). Others are making smaller changes. France’s state-owned railway operator, for instance, says it is adapting stations for extreme weather.

But it’s not possible to start from scratch.

“The challenge for us in Europe is, how do you go back and retrospectively adapt your infrastructure for a new age?,” said Mr. Mulcahey, who specializes in large-scale city planning.

On Thursday, a train derailed near Lewes, in southern England, injuring two, as Britain recorded its hottest day of the summer so far. It was not immediately clear whether the accident was heat related.

“But we do know that the rail companies have been reporting that the extreme dry conditions have been affecting embankments and track conditions,” James MacCleary, a lawmaker representing Lewes, told Times Radio on Thursday. “We had a lot of speed restrictions in the area recently, which is directly related to the heat.”

For trains, extreme heat poses three main problems:

Most aren’t air-conditioned. Europe is not known for air-conditioning — until recently, summers seldom got hot enough to need it with any regularity — and generally speaking, the continent’s trains are no exception.

That is changing, often as part of broader upgrades, but it is a slow and expensive process. London is spending an estimated £3.4 billion ($4.6 billion) to replace the carriages on another metro line, the Piccadilly, with a streamlined new fleet whose features include air-conditioning. And that is just one of the 11 lines in the city’s underground system, known as the Tube.

Mr. Mulcahey said Londoners were starting to modify their commutes to spend at least part of them on air-conditioned routes, like the Elizabeth Line or the city’s overground trains.

Discomfort aside, overheated trains can lead to heat exhaustion and worse. Many carriage windows don’t open, and if a train should lose power, the situation could become dangerous under a scorching sun. Although heat — like fire — can be deadly, it probably wouldn’t occur to passengers to use emergency hammers to break the windows, said Jennifer Schooling, a professor at Anglia Ruskin University and a director of DARe, a research center in Britain that studies the effects of global warming on transportation.

Heat can warp the tracks. Tracks are made of metal, which expands in the heat. Many of Europe’s were built decades ago, designed for less extreme temperatures, and lately they have been buckling and twisting.

A “sun curve” — that is, a rail bending sideways in extreme heat — is believed to have caused a freight train derailment in Sweden in June, the Swedish Transport Administration said.

Experts say a cheap adaptation to this problem is available by painting the tracks white, which creates a cooling effect by reflecting back sunlight. (Britain does this for “hot spots” on its rails.)

But that stopgap fix is no substitute for an expensive, wholesale replacement of track, said Prof. François Gemenne, the academic director of the master’s program in sustainability and social innovation at HEC Paris, a business school.

“You can win a couple of years with that,” Professor Gemenne said of lighter coloring. “But at some point, you will need to have rails that can withstand much higher temperatures.”

Power lines are vulnerable, too. The overhead wires that supply power to electric trains can expand in extreme heat, just as tracks do. Sometimes, older or badly maintained lines droop so low that they get caught on a moving train.

That can cause a power outage and, occasionally, a cascading series of problems along the rail network. “One incident can block a busy corridor, trap rolling stock and crews in the wrong locations and generate delays and cancellations,” Professor Geoffron said. One such incident in the Netherlands last month disrupted traffic between Britain, France, Belgium and Germany, he said.

Some newer cables have automated systems that adapt to temperature fluctuations, using balance weights or springs to loosen or tighten as needed. But the tension in older cables is fixed, and if they’re too tight, they can snap in the wintertime, Professor Schooling said.

“We’re in this conundrum,” she said. “The impacts of climate change seem to be happening faster than we were expecting.”

Many of Europe’s roads weren’t built for today’s extreme temperatures, either. Roads made with concrete can crack if they don’t have room to expand in the heat. Such “blowups” forced the partial closure of German highways this summer.

Road surfaces can melt, too, a phenomenon that has caused disruptions from Britain to Sweden. During Europe’s June heat wave, trams were halted in the German city of Leipzig because asphalt had melted and gummed up the tracks.

As with railroad tracks, lighter colors can keep road surfaces cooler, Professor Geoffron said. Roads can also be made with materials that are more heat resistant than traditional asphalt. But those materials are often more expensive and require more exacting construction, he said.

During recent heat waves, trucks that spread salt during winter storms laid down sand or dust on some English streets to keep melting road surfaces from getting too sticky.

Even that low-budget fix can be tricky, Professor Schooling said. Too much sand, and cars could start to skid.

item.title: Record-Breaking Rainfall Leaves Eight Dead and Thousands Stranded in Japan
item.description:
At least eight people have died in Japan after record-breaking rain set off flooding across a large region to the east of Tokyo, Japan’s public broadcaster said on Friday.

An intense storm pummeled the region, Chiba Prefecture, between Thursday and Friday, with nearly 350 millimeters of rainwater, about 13.7 inches, falling in just 12 hours on the regional capital, also called Chiba, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency. That was about three times the average total for the entire month of August, the prefecture’s governor said in a news conference on Friday, and the highest amount to fall on the area in 12 hours since observations began in 1976.

The meteorological agency had earlier issued a level-five emergency warning for heavy rain across 22 municipalities in Chiba Prefecture from Thursday night to early Friday morning, warning residents of “unprecedented heavy rainfall” and urging them to take immediate safety measures.

It was the first time that a level-five warning, the highest alert level, had been issued since the nation’s weather system was revised earlier this year for increased clarity. While the warnings were downgraded by Friday afternoon, the rainfall — which also caused mass power outages and widespread transportation disruptions — was expected to continue.

Japan’s public broadcaster, NHK, citing the Chiba police, said that in addition to the eight deaths many thousands had been left stranded as they tried to navigate the transportation turmoil.

Across the region there were scenes of chaos, with cars and buses submerged and water flooding into train stations and shopping centers. Footage from social media showed people in Chiba wading through waist-high water.

At Soga railway station in Chiba city, members of Japan’s military, the Self-Defense Forces, were dispatched early on Friday morning to provide transportation for about 4,000 people stranded around the station overnight.

Thousands were also left stranded at Narita International Airport in Chiba on Thursday night after train services to and from the airport were suspended. While flights operated as usual, train services remained disrupted through Friday.

According to Tokyo Electric Power Company, almost 20,000 homes in Chiba were still without power as of Friday afternoon.

The heavy rain came days after the severe tropical storm Chan-hom made landfall in the prefecture directly north of Chiba, adding to what has already been a summer of heightened storm activity and brutal heat.

item.title: Farage Wins Special U.K. Election That He Initiated, as Expected
item.description:
Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform U.K., Britain’s populist right-wing party, won a special election on Thursday that he initiated when he resigned amid a parliamentary investigation into possible financial impropriety.

As expected, Mr. Farage easily defeated dozens of fringe and novelty candidates, including Count Binface, who wears a trash-can-themed costume. None of Britain’s other major parties participated in the race, the results of which were announced early Friday. They called it a political stunt engineered by the Reform leader to distract from the investigation.

Mr. Farage received 22,239 votes, or 63 percent. Count Binface, a character played by Jon Harvey, 46, a writer and comedian, received 9,455 votes, or 27 percent. Mr. Binface’s previous best result was 1 percent in a London mayoral election.

Turnout was slightly higher than expected, with 35,401 voters — 44 percent of those eligible — participating in the election.

In a departure from political tradition in Britain, Mr. Farage did not attend the official announcement of the result. At a Reform U.K. event called “Farage Fest” a few hours earlier, he pre-emptively announced that he had won. And he told supporters: “I am damned if I am going to stand on a stage, having won a resounding victory, a ringing endorsement of all that I’ve tried to fight for and you’ve tried to fight for, and be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies.”

The Reform leader is under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner for failing to declare a 5 million pound gift, about $6.7 million, that he received in the weeks before the 2024 general election. Mr. Farage has given varying explanations for the gift, which he received from Christopher Harborne, a British crypto-billionaire based in Thailand. At one point Mr. Farage said it was a reward for Brexit, while at other times he has said it was to pay for his personal security.

Last month, Mr. Farage abruptly resigned the seat, which he had held since 2024, and immediately announced he would run again in the ensuing by-election, saying he wanted a new mandate from his constituents in Clacton, a coastal area in Essex, England, to show that his voters did not care about the allegations.

“The people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions,” he said in his resignation speech in July. “This will be a people-versus-the-establishment by-election.”

Mr. Farage referred in the speech to the standards investigation into the Harborne gift, and also said that “yet another standards investigation is underway.” Days before, The Sunday Times of London had reported that one of Mr. Farage’s close aides, George Cottrell, had provided undisclosed benefits to Mr. Farage, including security, social media employees and accommodation. Mr. Farage has since said he did not need to report the benefits because they were received before his election to Parliament.

The parliamentary code of conduct says that lawmakers must register any benefits received in the 12 months before they are elected, unless they could be considered “purely personal gifts.” It adds: “Both the possible motive of the giver and the use to which the gift is to be put should be considered. If there is any doubt, the benefit should be registered.”

Mr. Farage is an ally of President Trump who has long warned of an “invasion” of migrants and railed against “the establishment.” In May, Reform won almost 1,500 seats on municipal councils. But its overall share of the vote was only about 26 percent, down from more than 30 percent the previous year.

Several recent polls have shown support for the party falling to under 25 percent and Labour taking the lead. The polls have shown a continued decline as the accusations about improper disclosure of financial support have increased.

Reform officials were always very confident, however, that Mr. Farage would recapture his seat in Clacton, which voted by a large margin for Brexit, his signature cause. The last time he ran there, during the 2024 general election, he won with 46.2 percent of the vote, and the Conservative Party candidate came second with 27.9 percent.

item.title: American Missionary Kidnapped in Niger Soon to Be Reunited With Family
item.description:
A mission organization said on Friday that a pilot who was kidnapped while working for the group in the West African country of Niger last year was in “good health” after his release.

The missionary pilot, Kevin Rideout, was seized from his home in Niamey, the capital of Niger, in October. The organization, called Serving in Mission, said in a statement that Mr. Rideout was with U.S. officials as he waited to be reunited with his loved ones.

“We are grateful to confirm that our good friend and brother in Christ, Kevin Rideout, has been released,” the statement read. The mission added that he was in “good health in the care of U.S. officials” and would soon be reunited with his wife, Krista; their four children; and his extended family.

“Krista and the rest of Kevin’s family are profoundly grateful for the prayers offered on their behalf by people around the world throughout his captivity,” the statement added.

Mr. Rideout’s release was earlier reported by The New York Times based on the account of two U.S. officials, who spoke on Thursday on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters. How and where he was released were not yet clear, the officials said at the time, and it was also unclear which group had held him at the end of his captivity. Mr. Rideout’s release had been a major priority for the White House and for the military’s Africa Command.

In May, the French journalist and researcher Wassim Nasr, who has been monitoring jihadist groups in the area for several years, said that Mr. Rideout was being held in Ménaka, a region in Mali just over the border with Niger. That area is mostly controlled by a local branch of the Islamic State.

For years, Mali and Niger have been battling insurgents affiliated with Al Qaeda and the Islamic State. In April, Al Qaeda-linked militants launched coordinated attacks across Mali, seizing a major city and killing the country’s defense minister.

item.title: With Trump’s Hamas Deal in Peril, Kushner Set to Visit Israel for Gaza Talks
item.description:
Jared Kushner, President Trump’s senior aide and son-in-law, is set to visit Israel early next week, according to four people familiar with the plans, days after the Israeli government rejected a U.S.-brokered disarmament deal with Hamas.

Mr. Kushner is expected to meet with Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu to discuss Gaza, the people said, speaking on condition of anonymity to divulge details about Mr. Kushner’s schedule.

The deal, agreed to earlier this month between Mr. Trump’s Board of Peace and the militant group Hamas, called for the disarmament of Palestinian factions in Gaza and the withdrawal of Israeli forces there.

The Board of Peace is a new international organization chaired by Mr. Trump that has focused on plans for governing and rebuilding Gaza. Mr. Kushner is a senior member of its executive board and was involved in cease-fire negotiations between Hamas and Israel.

Mr. Netanyahu said Sunday that Israel rejected the deal, a move that was seen as an appeal to his right-wing voting base ahead of national elections in October. Yet the prime minister also ordered the Israeli military to pause its strikes in Gaza, in an apparent effort to appease the Trump administration.

For days after the announcement, the Israeli military conducted no airstrikes in Gaza, until Wednesday, when the military carried out a fresh attack, saying it was targeting Hamas militants. It conducted further attacks on Thursday.

Hamas officials have condemned the strikes, calling on mediating countries in the region to pressure Israel to halt them.

Hamas remains in control of about half of Gaza, where most of its people live. The group said that among those killed by Israel this week was the head of the police force in the Gaza City area.

Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace’s high representative for Gaza and former United Nations envoy, will join Mr. Kushner in Israel, according to two of the people with knowledge of the visit. Mr. Mladenov has played a leading role in the negotiations with Hamas over disarmament, frequently meeting with officials from the group in Egypt.

Mr. Kushner and Mr. Mladenov were also expected to visit Egypt next week to meet with regional mediators, according to two of the people.

The deal with Hamas says that, as part of the disarmament process, Israel should first uphold its side of the cease-fire, which was agreed to in October last year. That includes halting airstrikes and allowing more aid into Gaza.

The 15-point document leaves elements of the disarmament process vague, however. It calls for a “gradual, sequential and timebound manner” for decommissioning and storing heavy weapons, with an exact timetable still to be determined.

It adds that, at the “end of the process,” the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, will “hold, control or store weapons in Gaza.” The committee, a body of Palestinian technocrats, was assembled by the Board of Peace to take over governing Gaza under the board’s supervision.

Many Israelis remain skeptical that Mr. Trump’s Board of Peace can successfully disarm Hamas. The group has long touted armed struggle against Israel as the core of its ideology, and members have said they regard disarmament as tantamount to surrender.

item.title: One Sudanese City Is the Civil War’s Latest Battleground
item.description:
The Rapid Support Forces paramilitary group has pounded the city of El Obeid in south-central Sudan with drones for months. Its goal: wresting it from the Sudanese Army.

The State Department said in June that the paramilitary group was massing its forces around the city and that atrocities could occur if the R.S.F. took control. U.S. officials have warned that El Obeid may suffer the same fate as El Fasher, a major city in Darfur seized last October by the R.S.F., which committed massacres that the United Nations said bore the hallmarks of genocide.

The United Nations and the African Union have echoed those warnings about what could happen if the R.S.F. were to seize El Obeid.

The civil war in Sudan began in April 2023, when the leaders of the military and the R.S.F., which took power in a coup in 2021, fell out with one another. Since then, the conflict has caused one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with around 14 million people forced to flee their homes. Some estimates have put the death toll at 400,000. Military commanders have prohibited journalists from traveling to the area. Phone access remains difficult in many parts of the country.

El Obeid is strategically significant, with a highway running through the city that links Darfur, in west Sudan, to the east. A major pipeline in the city transports oil via the Kordofan region to Port Sudan on the Red Sea.

Taking El Obeid would enable the R.S.F. to consolidate its hold on western Sudan, after seizing El Fasher last year. Ahmed Tugud Lissan, a spokesman for the political alliance that is led by the R.S.F., said that the group planned to retake Khartoum, the Sudanese capital, once it had control of El Obeid.

El Obeid had a population of around half a million before the war, and while its present size is unknown, experts with the United Nations say the number of people there has most likely grown in recent months, with residents flocking to the city after fleeing violence elsewhere.

Several analysts said this week that the R.S.F. was unlikely to capture El Obeid in the short term. The Sudanese Army is in charge of defending the city and remains firmly in control.

The army seized three towns north of the city in recent weeks, opening up a supply route from Khartoum to El Obeid, which are more than 200 miles apart. “I don’t think it’s ever been that close to falling,” Alan Boswell, Horn of Africa director for the International Crisis Group, said of El Obeid.

Mr. Lissan, for his part, said that his group intended to capture the city and then march on Khartoum, though he acknowledged that it was far from achieving the initial goal.

Several analysts said there was evidence the R.S.F. had reduced the frequency of its strikes on El Obeid in recent weeks as drones attacks have become central to the war.

The R.S.F. has said that its drone strikes in the city have hit only military targets, but human rights groups say they have killed civilians and hit fuel depots and water plants, causing blackouts and water shortages.

Women are particularly vulnerable because of the attacks, according to a report last month by U.N. Women. The strikes have taken place during the day, forcing women and girls to collect water for households after dark. This has, in turn, led to a rise in rape and sexual assault cases, the report said.

El Fasher fell in October after a long siege, which ended when R.S.F. fighters swept into the city. They then filmed themselves conducting executions and massacres.

Now there’s fear of a repeat in El Obeid, though analysts said this week that the ethnic rivalries that drove the violence in El Fasher were less pronounced in El Obeid.

Human rights groups have accused the Trump administration, Britain and the European Union of not doing more to prevent the fall of El Fasher, and some said this week that the warnings on El Obeid in June had not been accompanied by concrete action to deter the R.S.F. from attacking the city.

In particular, they said, insufficient pressure had been put on the United Arab Emirates to stop suppling arms to the group. The New York Times and others have reported that the Emirates has supplied drones and other weapons to the R.S.F.

The Emirati foreign ministry has denied the allegations.

“What’s happening in El Obeid is a combination of global negligence and the weapons supplies coming from abroad,” said Mohamed Osman, a researcher with Human Rights Watch.

Both the R.S.F. and the Sudanese Army have been accused of committing atrocities and violating international law.

item.title: Heat is Hammering Europe, Again. Here’s What That Looks Like.
item.description:
For the fifth time this summer, Europe is sweating under an intense heat wave.

The signs of a persistently hot and exceptionally dry summer are everywhere. Brown, dusty patches have replaced verdant lawns in London’s parks. Major rivers like the Danube and the Rhine have retreated, exposing sandbars. The conditions have created a tinderbox for wildfires. Forests in Germany and in Bosnia and Herzegovina were ablaze on Friday, while firefighters were battling to save thousands of acres and hundreds of homes in Britain, France, Greece and Spain.

Weeks of relentless heat have tested the continent’s resolve, buckling train lines, shorting power grids and smashing records that had been set only recently. The combination of a “heat dome” phenomenon and the effects of climate change have left Europe wondering whether suffocating summers are the new norm.

item.title: Inside Russia’s Giant Push to Upend a Tiny Country
item.description:
It resembled in many ways a summer camp. Barbecues and beach volleyball games were on offer. A wellness spa was called “Relax and Have Fun.”

The men and women who attended the program at a resort complex in a remote part of Serbia also took part in more sinister activities, like learning to break through police cordons and set buildings on fire. They donned flak jackets and trained with assault rifles.

Their counselors, it turned out, were operatives with ties to Russia’s military intelligence service, known as the GRU. Their purpose, according to intelligence officials from three countries who described the activities, was to build a cadre of disciplined shock troops trained in election interference.

The target was tiny Moldova, a country of about three million people that carries outsize importance for President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

The Kremlin’s campaign included methods familiar elsewhere in the West, like hacking and disinformation. But in Moldova, its intervention went further than perhaps anywhere else outside Ukraine, and stands as one of the most extensive and audacious plots to date in Mr. Putin’s effort to destabilize the West, the three Western intelligence officials say.

Besides the camp in Serbia, Russian agents ran training programs in Bosnia and Moscow that were designed to turn pro-Russian Moldovans into foot soldiers. Moscow paid hundreds of Orthodox Moldovan priests to recruit voters and to push Russian narratives from the pulpit. And it spent hundreds of millions of dollars on a sophisticated vote-buying scheme financed by a Moldovan billionaire in exile and conceived and operated from Skolkovo, the Kremlin’s knockoff Silicon Valley outside Moscow.

Moscow’s campaign has not stopped. This spring, Russian missiles targeted energy infrastructure that provided service to Moldova, polluting waterways and disrupting electricity flows.

This article is based on interviews with activists who took part in the Russian effort; senior Moldovan law enforcement and security officials; and more than half a dozen European and American intelligence officials. The New York Times also reviewed thousands of documents related to Russia’s attempts to interfere in Moldova’s elections.

Many of those interviewed insisted on speaking anonymously, either to discuss sensitive security operations or because they feared retribution.

Details about Russian efforts in Moldova have emerged in court cases and local reporting, but the scope and extent of the campaign, including the vote-buying scheme and role of Russia’s intelligence services, has not been previously reported.

Publicly, Russian officials have denied interfering in Moldova’s affairs, and have dismissed accusations that Moscow is trying to undermine the West. Last December, Mr. Putin, in an address to military commanders, castigated European leaders for “stoking hysteria” over the threat from Russia.

Soon afterward, though, he gathered the leaders for a secret briefing to deliver the exact opposite message, according to officials from two countries with knowledge of the episode. Their goal for 2026, Mr. Putin told them, is “the collapse of NATO and the E.U. from within,” the people said.
